title: Around 2011, fewer than one farmer in ten borrowed from banks while about a quarter were barred by old arrears; repeated debt write-offs since 1999 have not broken the cycle

rootCauses.cause: Credit allocated administratively: 'supervised credit' from budget funds for cereal smallholders, decided by local authorities, with no bank risk-taking and a 38% repayment rate
Repeated state write-offs and reschedulings (Law 99-65 of 1999, Finance Law 2014, Law 2026-5) with no permanent legal framework for over-indebted farmers
Bank eligibility rules exclude anyone with overdue debt; missing or uncertain land titles are cited as a collateral barrier (asserted, not tested; see FND-TG-781)
Institutional credit risk is uninsured against drought: only about 7% of farmers are insured and drought is not covered, so a bad year can turn loans into arrears

Agricultural investment trend after 2012 (APIA investment statistics, ONAGRI) not sourced here.
No sourced projection of farm debt or credit access.
author: TahaGHZ
excerpt: Formal credit reached very few Tunisian farmers around 2010-2012: no more than 7% had bank loans, banks financed 11% of agricultural investment, and seasonal credit covered one-fourteenth of input use. At the same time…

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content: Formal credit reached very few Tunisian farmers around 2010-2012: no more than 7% had bank loans, banks financed 11% of agricultural investment, and seasonal credit covered one-fourteenth of input use (SRC-TG-925). At the same time about 120,000 farmers (23% of the total) were listed in the credit registry as defaulters and barred from new formal loans. The study found total overdue agricultural loans of about TND 750 million, TND 708 million of it at the state-owned BNA (SRC-TG-925). In a separate BCT series that uses a different definition, unpaid and litigation agricultural loans across banks rose from TND 477 million in December 2010 to TND 705 million in December 2016 (SRC-TG-926). Lack of investment follows. The share of farmers whose credit demand was satisfied fell from 54% (1990-94) to 36% (2000-04), and the share investing from 36% to 26% (SRC-TG-925). In March 2026 another regularisation law was enacted, Law 2026-5 (SRC-TG-932). Tier C reporting of a BCT statement puts 33,535 agricultural actors in categories 4-5 at public banks in June 2025, including 28,750 individuals and 4,785 firms (SRC-TG-933).

sections.heading: Root causes
sections.content:
**Symptom versus cause.** Low credit use and high arrears are symptoms. The sources point to four causes.

1. **Administered credit (legacy).** Under the "supervised credit" system, cereal smallholders received BNA loans from budget funds based on standard requirements, with local authorities deciding and the BNA bearing no risk. Repayment averaged 38%, against 73% for comparable BNA own-risk loans (SRC-TG-925). Seasonal credit for smallholders was in practice limited to cereals: vegetables had no direct seasonal loans after 2004 and tree crops none after 2001 (SRC-TG-925). This links to the cereal bias of support policy (FND-TG-921).
2. **Repeated write-offs without a framework (legacy).** Law 99-65 of 15 July 1999 covered loans funded from state budget resources or external credit borrowed directly by the state. It wrote off principal and interest on qualifying agricultural loans up to TND 2,000 per farmer obtained before 1999 (ceiling TND 100 million). For loans of TND 2,000-40,000 it waived late interest and half of contractual interest; the state repaid banks over 20 years for written-off principal up to TND 2,000, while banks could deduct 50% of waived interest from taxable profit for the TND 2,000-40,000 band (SRC-TG-927). Finance Law 2014 (Law 2013-54) reportedly waived principal and interest on agricultural loans obtained up to December 2012 (tier C; official text not opened; SRC-TG-928). SRC-TG-929 is cited only as reporting the legal basis for BNA write-offs. The minister put beneficiaries at over 80,000 farmers and the amount at over TND 115 million (SRC-TG-928, tier C). Since 2012 several write-offs for small farmers and fishers have been made under finance laws (SRC-TG-926). Law 2026-5 of 11 March 2026 obliges all banks to reschedule category 4+ agricultural debts classified before 30 September 2025 over up to seven years, including one grace year. It waives late penalties against a 5% down payment. Debtors who pay in full within six months also get 50% of the original contractual interest waived. The Central Bank must then automatically delete the beneficiaries' negative classifications (SRC-TG-932). Press reported the early-payment benefit as a 50% discount on amounts due, including contractual interest (SRC-TG-930); the law limits it to 50% of original contractual interest plus late penalties. The 2012 World Bank study already listed "repeated debt cancellations and rescheduling" among measures that had not improved access. It noted that Tunisia has no legal framework for debt negotiation or adjustment for over-indebted persons (SRC-TG-925). The sources do not test whether expected amnesties reduce repayment, so that link is a hypothesis, not a finding.
3. **Eligibility and collateral.** Any overdue debt makes a farmer ineligible. The 2017 AICS study concludes that indebtedness has become "a real factor of exclusion" from institutional finance, and it also cites missing or uncertain land titles (SRC-TG-926). FND-TG-781 shows that the title-to-credit link is widely asserted but not tested with data.
4. **Uninsured climate risk.** Only about 7% of farmers are insured (35,000 of 516,000 holdings), insurance is usually a condition for a bank loan, and drought, the main hazard, is not covered (SRC-TG-925, SRC-TG-926). About a quarter of surveyed farmers do not ask for credit for fear of indebtedness (SRC-TG-925).

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.content:
- 7% of farmers with bank loans; banks fund 11% of investment, own resources 70%, state grants about 20%. BNA provides 36% of bank lending to agriculture (SRC-TG-925, para. 1-2). The 2017 AICS report repeats the 7% figure (SRC-TG-926, p. 51). This is one data point, not a trend.
- 120,000 farmers (23%) indebted and barred. TND 750 million overdue, TND 708 million at BNA. 78% of BNA overdue cases average under TND 5,000 and total TND 260 million. Many loans have been overdue for over ten years (SRC-TG-925, para. 28).
- Agriculture's share of direct bank lending fell from above 9% to below 4% over 2003-2008, while total bank lending rose 58% (SRC-TG-925, para. 34).
- In the 2008/09 season fewer than 5,000 farmers, under 1% of the total, received direct bank input loans (SRC-TG-925, para. 33).
- BCT risk registry: farmers and fishers recorded for agricultural credit numbered 111,785 (Dec 2010) and 119,031 (Dec 2014), then 80,758 (Dec 2015) and 61,355 (May 2017) (SRC-TG-926, Tableau 13). AICS reads these as farmers who received credit and attributes the fall to loan refusals and abstention (SRC-TG-926). Two points cut against that reading. The 2010-2014 level (112,000-119,000) is close to the 120,000 indebted farmers in the 2012 study (SRC-TG-925), and far above the roughly 36,000 farmers that 7% of 516,000 holdings would imply. The sharp drop in 2015 also coincides with the Finance Law 2014 write-off. Our inference is that the series largely tracks the indebted stock, and that part of the fall reflects written-off loans leaving the registry rather than fewer borrowers. The source does not examine this.
- Unpaid and litigation agricultural loans, all banks and leasing: TND 477 million (2010), 629 million (2013), 705 million (2016), 671 million (May 2017). The private bank share rose from TND 47 million to 123 million (SRC-TG-926, Tableau 14).
- 2026 (tier C): La Presse reports more than 33,000 farmers excluded from bank finance, an estimated TND 4.4 billion with 21.5% classified, and agriculture below 7% of BNA's portfolio (SRC-TG-931). The TND 4.4 billion / 21.5% figures were presented at a parliamentary study day in January 2026; they likely refer to outstanding agricultural credit rather than arrears. Tunisie Numérique separately quotes BCT figures of about TND 4.6 billion outstanding at end-November 2025 and 33,535 high-risk actors at public banks in June 2025 (SRC-TG-933).

**Disagreements.** BNA overdue agricultural loans around 2011 are TND 708 million in the World Bank study (SRC-TG-925), but TND 419-440 million for 2011-2012 in the BNA/BCT series reported by AICS (SRC-TG-926). All-bank totals also differ: about TND 750 million (SRC-TG-925) against TND 477-540 million for 2010-2011 (SRC-TG-926). The definitions probably differ (all overdue amounts including interest vs unpaid plus litigation), but neither source says so. Both sets of values are recorded.

**Stock versus flow.** The 7% (current borrowers) and the 23% (farmers carrying old arrears) are compatible. The arrears are an old stock, often over ten years old (SRC-TG-925), that excludes people from new borrowing.

**BNA exposure to the state cereal system.** In February 2024 the Office des Céréales owed TND 6,343 million to commercial banks, 83% of it to the BNA, because CGC compensation payments arrive late (SRC-TG-705). The same bank is the main lender to farmers and holds most overdue farm loans (SRC-TG-925, SRC-TG-926). The sources do not show whether OC lending crowds out BNA lending to farmers. That link is a question for further research, not a finding.

sections.heading: Why confidence is what it is
sections.content: Medium. The core diagnosis comes from a detailed World Bank/FAO/AFD study (SRC-TG-925), corroborated by BCT and BNA data in a 2017 consultancy report (SRC-TG-926), and the 1999 and 2026 laws are documented by the official gazette (SRC-TG-927, SRC-TG-932). The farmer-level figures are about 15 years old, and the access share has not been remeasured. The Finance Law 2014 write-off, 2026 classified-actor count and outstanding-credit figures rely on tier C reporting of official statements (SRC-TG-928, SRC-TG-933). Those parts carry low confidence on their own.

sections.heading: Links to other sectors
sections.content:
- **Water.** Investment grants of up to 60% are offered for water-saving equipment (SRC-TG-925, para. 29), but farmers who cannot get bank credit cannot finance their share. This record does not quantify the effect on irrigation modernisation; the water lane covers irrigation efficiency.
- **Energy.** None found.

sections.heading: Leads for phase 2
sections.content:
- Law n° 99-65 of 15 July 1999 on agricultural and fishing debt (SRC-TG-927): https://faolex.fao.org/docs/pdf/tun18563.pdf
- Finance Law 2014 (Law n° 2013-54) agricultural debt write-off (SRC-TG-929).
- Law n° 2026-5 of 11 March 2026 on regularising distressed agricultural debts (SRC-TG-932): https://arp.tn/ar_SY/document/download/117527
- Finance Law 2026 article 59 agricultural debt measure (reported in the press; text not opened).
- Banque Tunisienne de Solidarité individual loans and microcredit associations (SRC-TG-925, para. 30).
- SOTUGAR / Fonds National de Garantie loan guarantees (SRC-TG-925).
- Indirect lending through agribusinesses and grain buyers, which grew 59% over 2004-2008 (SRC-TG-925, para. 34).
- Agricultural insurance (CTAMA), the 50% premium subsidy for hail on cereals, and the missing drought cover (SRC-TG-926).
- APIA investment grants under Decree n° 94-427 (SRC-TG-924, SRC-TG-925).
- World Bank 2012 Agricultural Finance Study recommendations on microfinance, risk management and producer organisations (SRC-TG-925).

resolvedSources.title: Project Paper on a proposed additional loan of US$300 million for a Second Additional Financing to the Tunisia Emergency Food Security Response Project (Report PAD5602)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Dated March 1, 2024. Sectoral context, para 8, p. 3:

> For the fourth consecutive year, below-average rainfall and extreme heat have combined to dramatically compromise Tunisia's grain production in 2022/23. As shown in Table 1 below, the Grain Board collected less than half of durum wheat quantities in 2023 compared to average drought years 2020-22 and two-thirds less than in a non-drought year (such as 2019), and almost no barley (1.3 percent of average drought years).

Table 1, "Grain quantities collected by OC (2019-2023)", '000 t, source Tunisia Grain Board (OC), rows (2019 / average 2020-2022 / 2023):

> Durum wheat 876.4 685.6 286.7
> Soft wheat 75.4 31.3 6.2
> Barley 332.9 39.5 0.5
> Total 1284.7 756.4 293.4

Para 8, p. 3 (continued):

> Consequently, average monthly grain import needs have skyrocketed (100,000 MT/month for durum wheat and 100,000 MT/month for barley, currently estimated at US$48 million/month for durum wheat and US$28 million/month for barley).

Footnote 15:

> This is particularly true in Tunisia where people remember vividly the bread riots that occurred from December 1983 to January 1984, triggered by a temporary rise in the price of bread due to the government austerity program.

Para 9, p. 3:

> For the period from July 2023 to June 2024, the Grain Board is facing an additional financing gap of around US$522 million due to very low local harvest of durum wheat and barley.

Footnote to Table 2, p. 4:

> Soft wheat import needs are not substantially impacted by drought since Tunisia is 95 percent dependent on imports.

Box 1, p. 4:

> The Grain Board (OC) is an SOE created in 1962 under the tutelage of Ministry of Agriculture, Water Resources and Fisheries (MAWRF) with a core mandate to regulate and ensure a stable supply of grain on the domestic market through domestic grain harvest collection, imports, and the management of strategic reserves.

> The OC has a de jure monopoly over grain trade (domestic collection and imports), except for barley (animal feed) for which domestic collection (traditionally) and imports (since April 2023) have been authorized for selected private operators.

> The OC buys grain domestically at farmgate prices fixed annually by a government decree. These prices have been below import-parity prices; they were increased by around 60 percent since 2022 to incentivize production.

> The OC sells the grain it purchases at subsidized prices to the millers who are granted specific acquisition quotas; the millers in turn sell the milled products (soft wheat bread flour, soft wheat pastry flour, durum semolina) to bakeries and processors similarly at subsidized prices under quota assignments. End products (such as bread, pasta, and couscous) are sold to consumers at subsidized prices.

> Because of CGC protracted payments, OC must resort to financing by the National Agriculture Bank which is difficult to mobilize and costly.

> CGC, a state-owned entity created in 1970, is responsible for providing compensatory payments to operators at the different segments of the grain value chain to cover the gap between market and administered prices.

Footnote 3:

> Farmgate gate prices in 2023 have been increased by 60.9 percent, 64.2 percent and 60.7 percent for durum wheat, soft wheat and barley respectively, compared to 2021. In February 2024, official farmgate prices for durum wheat and barley are respectively 3 percent sand 14 percent lower than OC import cost (Source OC).

Box 1 continued, p. 5:

> (iii) there are illegal and improper use of subsidized grain products, i.e., improper use of semolina for feed to animals, illegal leakages of grain products towards neighboring countries, as well as excessive consumption and wastage of bread and wheat-based products by end-consumers, e.g., wastage of 900,000 "baguettes" daily; and (iv) the system limits the active participation of the private sector

Para 10, p. 5:

> For calendar years 2022 and 2023, the OC was supposed to receive TND6,625 million (Tunisian Dinar) – i.e., approximately US$2,106 million - from the CGC, but funding effectively received from the compensation fund was only 38 percent (i.e., TND2,543 million or US$808 million).

> As of February 2024, the OC's estimated overall 2023 balance (yet to be audited) amounts to TND -900 million (equivalent to US$ -286 million) and OC's total debt to commercial banks is TND6,343 million (equivalent to US$2,016 million, out of which 83 percent towards the National Agriculture Bank - BNA).

Para 11, p. 5:

> the GoT is carrying out a series of measures that, if fully implemented, would lead to a more sustainable sector and sizeable budget savings in the range of US$400-600 million per year.

Para 10, p. 5 (continued):

> This situation makes it very difficult for OC to access additional financing from commercial banks for grain imports

Para 13:

> This series of reforms would lead to OC's budget and fiscal savings estimated at US$576 million per year

Table 3, "Summary reform measures of the grain value chain and associated savings", measure names (rows extracted as text; fiscal columns not used):

> 4 Strengthening of compensation for losses (FIDAC) [...] Approved (2024 Fiscal Law)- December 31, 2023
> 5 Improved access to seasonal credit for grain producers [...] Approved (2024 Fiscal Law)- December 31, 2023
> 9 Liberalization of soft wheat imports for industrial processing of pastry flour (PS-7) [...] Planned: Cabinet Council to review the draft Decision

Footnote 4 (to Table 3 measure "Strengthening of compensation for losses (FIDAC)", approved in the 2024 Fiscal Law):

> FIDAC (Fonds d'Indemnisation des Dommages Agricoles causés par les Calamités naturelles): is a farmers' compensation fund in case of natural disaster, including drought.

Results framework, p. 43:

> Food subsidy reform implementation plan prepared [...] Preparation of a reform plan for food subsidies and switch to cash transfer, including consultation and communication.

Footnote 17:

> 43.3 percent of bread subsidy for "Gros pain" and 43.5 percent of subsidy for other staple durum wheat-based products go to the poorest two quintiles of Tunisia households in 2022.
resolvedSources.notes: Donor project document; figures on OC finances are sourced to the OC itself and are unaudited. Table 1 rows extracted cleanly; Table 2 (financing gap) extracted with shifted columns and is not used except for its footnote. Table 3 lists nine reform measures (barley import liberalisation April 2023, farmgate price increases, PS-7 flour taxation, planned soft wheat import liberalisation for pastry flour) — recorded as phase 2 leads only.

resolvedSources.title: Examen des politiques commerciales - Rapport du Secrétariat - Tunisie (WT/TPR/S/341)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Para. 3.167-3.169:

> La dernière notification de la Tunisie à l'OMC en matière de commerce d'État au sens de l'article XVII du GATT date de 2006. Elle indique la présence de neuf entreprises commerciales d'État. En 2004, 16% des importations tunisiennes était le fait d'entreprises commerciales d'État. Il n'a pas été possible d'obtenir une estimation de la part correspondante en 2015.
>
> Selon cette notification, l'Office du commerce de Tunisie (OCT) importe du sucre (en monopole de fait) et, sans droits exclusifs, le thé (noir et vert), le café vert et certains "produits conjoncturels" (principalement des pommes de terre et du riz), et procède à leur distribution en gros.
>
> L'Office des céréales exerce le monopole d'importation du blé dur, du blé tendre, et de l'orge. [...] L'Office national des huiles (ONH) importe des huiles de graines (soja, colza, olive) et exporte de l'huile d'olive, sans droits exclusifs

English gloss: Tunisia's last GATT Article XVII state-trading notification dates from 2006 and lists nine state trading enterprises; in 2004 they accounted for 16% of Tunisian imports. According to that notification, OCT imports sugar (de facto monopoly) and, without exclusive rights, tea, green coffee and some "conjunctural products" (mainly potatoes and rice). The Cereals Office holds the import monopoly for durum wheat, soft wheat and barley. ONH imports seed oils and exports olive oil without exclusive rights.

Para. 4.32-4.33:

> De nombreuses entreprises publiques continuent de concurrencer le secteur privé dans la production et le commerce agroalimentaire; certaines ont des positions exclusives dans la commercialisation, y compris à l'importation et à l'exportation. [...] L'État tunisien continue d'intervenir dans le secteur agroalimentaire en fixant les prix à la consommation (par exemple pain, farine, couscous, huile, sucre, lait et thé); le prix de revient industriel (par exemple sel, levure, café, bière); ou les marges de distribution (riz, volaille, oeufs, nombreux fruits et légumes et préparations alimentaires, tableau 3.20).

English gloss: many state enterprises still compete with the private sector in agri-food production and trade, some with exclusive marketing positions including import and export. The state still fixes consumer prices (bread, flour, couscous, oil, sugar, milk, tea), industrial cost prices, or distribution margins (rice, poultry, eggs, many fruits and vegetables).

Para. 4.34:

> l'Office des céréales est chargé d'acheter, sur le marché local, le blé dur et le blé tendre à des prix fixés par l'État. [...] Les charges liées au subventionnement par les pouvoirs publics des prix à la consommation pour les seules céréales s'élevaient à 170 millions de dinars en 2004; elles sont passées à 1 360 millions de dinars (plus de 600 millions d'euros) en 2014.

English gloss: the Cereals Office buys local durum and soft wheat at state-fixed prices. Consumer price subsidies for cereals alone rose from TND 170 million (2004) to TND 1,360 million (2014).

Para. 4.35:

> L'Office des céréales disposait jusqu'en 2016 du monopole d'importation du blé dur et tendre [...] Depuis janvier 2016, le droit de douane a été réduit à zéro sur les importations de blé. Selon les autorités, les importations de blé hors-contingent par le secteur privé sont désormais à taux zéro.

English gloss: the Cereals Office held the durum and soft wheat import monopoly until 2016; since January 2016 the wheat import duty is zero and, according to the authorities, out-of-quota private imports are now duty-free.

Para. 4.41:

> L'Office du commerce détient encore le monopole de l'importation au sein de ce CT, et délivre les autorisations d'importation de sucre.

English gloss: OCT still holds the import monopoly within the sugar tariff quota and issues sugar import authorisations.

Para. 4.48:

> L'ONH garantit un prix minimum aux producteurs qui, pour une raison ou une autre, n'ont pu avoir une meilleure offre pour écouler leur production. L'ONH achète cependant l'huile d'olive auprès des producteurs à un prix librement négocié.

English gloss: ONH guarantees a minimum price to producers who could not get a better offer for their output; ONH otherwise buys olive oil from producers at freely negotiated prices.

Para. 4.12:

> La dernière notification de la Tunisie à l'OMC en matière de soutien interne porte sur 2014.
resolvedSources.notes: Secretariat report, written in French, for Tunisia's third trade policy review. Paras. 3.168-3.169 describe the 2006 state-trading notification ("Selon cette notification"), so the present tense there reflects 2006; para. 4.35 updates this to 2016 (monopoly held "until 2016"). The apparent contradiction is a difference of reference date. Gives no PSE/NRA estimate.

resolvedSources.title: Tunisia Agricultural Finance Study: Main Summary Report (Report No. 62471-TN)
resolvedSources.publisher: World Bank, Sustainable Development Department, MENA Region (with FAO and AFD)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Executive summary, para. 4 (p. 7) and Part A, para. 1:

> Access to agricultural finance in Tunisia is limited. The portion of farmers benefitting from bank loans does not exceed 7 percent. Banks finance just 11 percent of total agricultural investment, while 70 percent—according to official statistics—is financed by "own resources", which probably includes a significant volume of supplier and purchaser credit. And this is despite several measures adopted by the Government of Tunisia (GoT) in recent years in support of the financing of agriculture: repeated debt cancellations and rescheduling, creation of new mechanisms for agriculture financing [...] Close to a quarter of agricultural enterprises are in arrears to the banks, of which the vast majority are small farmers. Only 7 percent of farmers are formally covered by some form of agricultural insurance, which is nearly always a condition for a bank loan, and no coverage exists against drought, which is the main natural hazard in Tunisia.

Part A, para. 2:

> The share of investment funded by credit has halved over the last 5 years. While only 11 percent of agricultural investment is financed by bank credit, about 20 percent is financed by state "encouragements", or investment subsidies. Seasonal credit only covers 1/14th of agricultural input use. A single bank, the state-owned BNA, is responsible for 36 percent of bank lending to agriculture. [...] When surveyed, about a quarter of farmers say that they do not request credit for fear of indebtedness and another quarter because of difficulties in accessing credit. The share of farmers reporting that their credit demand was satisfied fell from 54 percent in 1990-4 to 36 percent in 2000-4. The share of farmers investing fell from 36 percent to 26 percent over the same period.

Para. 28 (pp. 15-16):

> Indebtedness of farmers. About 120,000 farmers (23% of the total) are indebted to a financial institution. As a consequence, they are listed as debtors in the credit registry and barred from further loans from formal financial institutions. In addition, they cannot sell some of their crops to marketing organizations and POs, which deduct amounts due by the farmer to a bank and remit this to the creditor. The total value of overdue agricultural loans is about TND 750 million, of which 110,000 cases worth TND 708 million are from the BNA alone. In the case of BNA loans, 78% of the number of overdue loans involve an average amount below TND 5000 (≈ USD 3300), which adds up to TND 260 million (≈ USD 170 million). [...] Many of these loans have been overdue for more than ten years. Few farmers have accepted the offers of debt rescheduling after the two most recent droughts [...] Tunisia does not have a legal framework governing procedures for debt negotiations, debt counseling or debt adjustment for over-indebted persons.

Para. 29 (p. 16), list of government subsidies:

> (viii) direct investment grants for all types of investments in agriculture up to 25% of the investment cost; (ix) direct investment grants for specific investment categories, e.g. for water rationalization, up to 60% of the investment cost [...] The total costs and opportunity losses of these subsidies are not known as they are covered under different GoT budgets, which are not all publicly accessible, but certainly exceed TND 100 million per year. In addition, the costs of administering these subsidy programs are quite high, estimated at 15-18% of the value of the subsidies.

Para. 30 (p. 16):

> Over the past 15 years, 340,000 grants worth TND 1.1 billion have been disbursed in the different categories, supporting investments of TND 5.1 billion. Across all sizes of projects, 66% of total investment costs were funded by the investors themselves, 22% through the government grants program and only 13% through bank loans.

Para. 33 (p. 17):

> Tunisia operates a system of 'supervised credit', through which smallholders engaged in cereal production receive loans from the BNA based on standard requirements, and not on individual loan appraisal [...] in reality the local government authorities make the decisions which the BNA then implements. [...] Statistics from the Ministry of Finance over the past decade show an average repayment rate on these loans of 38%, which compares to a repayment rate of 73% for the loans to a similar clientele from BNA resources and on BNA risk. [...] For the 2008/09 season, less than 5000 farmers received direct bank loans for inputs, which is less than one percent of all farmers [...] Vegetable production has not received any direct seasonal loans since 2004, tree crops not since 2001 and other crops not since 2000.

Para. 34-35 (p. 17):

> Direct bank lending to clients for agricultural purposes, for which BNA is the prime provider, has declined by 28% over the period from 2003 to 2008. [...] Against this, total bank lending increased by 58% over the same period [...] The share of direct lending to agriculture in total lending therefore declined from above 9% to below 4%. Against this trend, indirect lending approaches (for example, through intermediaries such as agribusinesses and grain buyers) have gained in importance (+ 59% from 2004-2008). [...] the importance of agricultural loans in total lending has declined over the years, from 8-10% at the beginning of the decade to about 4-5% at present.

Para. 23 (credit guarantees):

> The country runs two guarantee mechanisms: one, the FNG, covering micro and small loans including those for agricultural purposes; and the other one, the SOTUGAR, targeted at the operations of the much larger loans. The FNG management was transferred to SOTUGAR in 2010. The FNG covers 90% of short, medium and long term loans of banks to small and medium farmers and fishermen and all loans granted by the BTS and the MCAs. [...] However, the Fund only pays out on claims once a financial institution has exhausted all means of recovery.
resolvedSources.notes: Field work 2010-2011. The farmer counts derive from the 2004-05 farm structure survey (about 516,000 holdings). Internal inconsistencies: bank-sector NPLs are given as 13% in the executive summary and 16% in the main text (not used here); the 11% (para. 1) and 13% (para. 30) bank share of investment refer to different bases (all agricultural investment vs. projects receiving grants). The "credit demand satisfied" series cites earlier surveys (1990-94, 2000-04).

resolvedSources.title: Analyse des Instruments de Financement du Secteur Agricole en Tunisie (rapport d'étude)
resolvedSources.publisher: ADVI for the Agenzia Italiana per la Cooperazione allo Sviluppo (AICS), Tunis
resolvedSources.extracts:
p. 34 (BNA, Tableau 7, source BNA 2017):

> Les impayés ont atteint 414 MDT, jusqu'à mai 2017, contre 461 MDT en 2016.

Tableau 7 "Evolution des impayés et contentieux" (MDT): déc-10 383; déc-11 419; déc-12 440; déc-13 457; déc-14 478; déc-15 444; déc-16 461; mai-17 414.

English gloss: BNA unpaid agricultural loans and litigation reached TND 414 million by May 2017, against TND 461 million in 2016.

p. 49 (Tableau 13, source BCT):

> Le nombre des exploitants agriculteurs et de pêcheurs déclarés à la centrale des risques, ayant bénéficié d'un crédit agricole a en effet tendance à régresser d'environ 50% depuis 2014 en passant de 119 milles exploitants à 61,3 milles exploitants en mai 2017.

Tableau 13 rows: déc-10 111 785; déc-11 115 283; déc-12 116 453; déc-13 118 635; déc-14 119 031; déc-15 80 758; déc-16 75 621; mai-17 61 355.

English gloss: the number of farmers and fishers recorded at the central bank risk registry as having received agricultural credit fell by about 50% from 119,000 (2014) to 61,300 (May 2017).

p. 49:

> Deux raisons à cette régression, à savoir le refus d'octroi des crédits et le comportement d'abstention de certains agriculteurs aux crédits agricoles.

> En effet, une bonne majorité des exploitants ne disposent pas de titres de propriété ou, à la limite, ils ne disposent que de titres incertains. [...] l'éligibilité de l'exploitant au crédit est conditionnée par l'inexistence des dettes échues et impayées. Il apparaît, donc, que l'endettement devient un véritable facteur d'exclusion des exploitants du financement institutionnel. En 2016, le total des impayés a atteint 705 millions de DT et en mai 2017 le cumul des impayés a été de 671 millions de DT.

English gloss: the decline has two reasons, loan refusals and farmers abstaining. Most farmers have no or uncertain land titles; eligibility requires no overdue debt, so indebtedness has become a real factor of exclusion. Total unpaid agricultural loans reached TND 705 million in 2016 and TND 671 million in May 2017.

p. 50 (Tableau 14, source BCT, unpaid and litigation by bank, MDT): Total déc-10 477; déc-11 540; déc-12 583; déc-13 629; déc-14 673; déc-15 669; déc-16 705; mai-17 671 (of which BNA 383 ... 414; private banks 47 ... 123).

> Depuis l'année 2012, plusieurs abandons de crédits au profit des petits agriculteurs et pêcheurs ont été effectués en application des dispositions des lois de finance (BCT, 2017)

English gloss: since 2012, several write-offs for small farmers and fishers were carried out under finance laws.

p. 51:

> Ce qui limite la proportion d'agriculteurs bénéficiant de prêts bancaires qui ne dépasse pas 7 %. D'ailleurs c'est le même taux qui représente les agriculteurs assurés, 35 mille agriculteurs assurés sur un nombre total de 516 mille exploitations soit un taux de l'ordre de 7% seulement.

English gloss: the share of farmers with bank loans does not exceed 7%; the same share are insured (35,000 of 516,000 holdings).

p. 51:

> Pour le risque de grêle sur les céréales, la prime est subventionnée à 50% (ONAGRI, 2015).
>
> Cependant, la sécheresse ne fait pas partie des risques couverts, alors qu'en Tunisie, cet aléa est le plus fréquent.

English gloss: the hail insurance premium for cereals is 50% subsidised; drought, the most frequent hazard, is not covered.
resolvedSources.notes: Consultancy report (dated August 2017 inside; file name says 2018). The 7% figure very likely repeats the World Bank 2012 study (SRC-TG-925) rather than being a new measurement. The drop in the risk registry count between Dec 2014 and Dec 2015 coincides with the Finance Law 2014 write-off; part of the fall may be cleared records rather than fewer borrowers. The report itself does not discuss this. Tables 7 and 14 show BNA at the same values, presumably the same series from different sources.

resolvedSources.title: Loi n° 99-65 du 15 juillet 1999, relative à l'examen de l'endettement du secteur de l'agriculture et de la pêche (JORT du 16 juillet 1999, pp. 1178-1179)
resolvedSources.publisher: Journal Officiel de la République Tunisienne (copy hosted by FAO FAOLEX)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Article premier (p. 1178):

> L'Etat abandonne les montants dus en principal et intérêt au titre des crédits agricoles obtenus jusqu'au 31 décembre 1998 et dont le montant total en principal n'excède pas deux mille dinars par agriculteur à la date de leur obtention et qui ont été accordés sur des ressources budgétaires ou sur des crédits extérieurs empruntés directement par l'Etat, et ce, dans la limite de cent millions de dinars (100 000 000 dinars).

English gloss: the state writes off principal and interest on agricultural loans obtained up to 31 December 1998 whose total principal does not exceed TND 2,000 per farmer, granted from budget resources or external loans borrowed by the state, up to a ceiling of TND 100 million.

Art. 2 (p. 1179):

> L'Etat abandonne le montant total des intérêts de retard et 50% du montant des intérêts conventionnels relatifs aux crédits agricoles obtenus jusqu'au 31 décembre 1998 et dont le montant total en principal est compris entre deux mille dinars et quarante mille dinars par agriculteur [...] dans la limite de cinquante cinq millions de dinars (55000000 dinars).

English gloss: for loans with principal between TND 2,000 and 40,000 per farmer, the state writes off all late interest and 50% of contractual interest, up to TND 55 million.

Art. 3 (p. 1179):

> L'Etat prend en charge les créances en principal abandonnées par les banques et relatives au reliquat des montants des crédits agricoles obtenus jusqu'au 31 décembre 1998 et dont le montant total en principal n'excède pas deux mille dinars [...] Les montants abandonnés [...] seront remboursés sur 20 ans sans intérêts à partir de l'an 2000, et ce, dans la limite de quarante millions de dinars (40 000 000 dinars)

English gloss: the state takes over principal written off by banks on loans up to TND 2,000, repaying the banks over 20 years interest-free from 2000, up to TND 40 million.

Art. 4 (p. 1179):

> Les banques peuvent déduire de l'assiette soumise à l'impôt sur les sociétés 50% des intérêts conventionnels abandonnés et relatifs aux crédits agricoles de campagne obtenus jusqu'au 31 décembre 1998 [...]

English gloss: banks may deduct 50% of waived contractual interest on qualifying seasonal agricultural loans from the corporate income-tax base.
resolvedSources.notes: Official gazette text (scanned; accents restored in the extracts). This is the earliest agricultural debt write-off law found in this research; it sets the template (amount threshold per farmer, cut-off date, state compensation of banks, tax deduction for banks in art. 4) reused in later measures.

resolvedSources.title: Tunisie - Economie : Plus de 80 000 agriculteurs concernés par l'abandon de la dette
resolvedSources.extracts:
Article of 22 January 2015, quoting the Minister of Agriculture Lassaad Lachaal (Béja, 21 January 2015):

> plus de 80.000 agriculteurs pour un montant dépassant 115 millions de dinars

English gloss: more than 80,000 farmers, for an amount above TND 115 million.

On the legal basis (loi de finances 2014):

> l'Etat renonce au principal et aux intérêts au titre des crédits agricoles obtenus à la fin de décembre 2012 [...] dont le montant dépasse (principal) 5.000 dinars

English gloss: the state waives principal and interest on agricultural loans obtained up to end December 2012 "whose amount exceeds (principal) TND 5,000".
resolvedSources.notes: Tier C. The threshold wording ("dépasse", exceeds) is doubtful: search-result summaries of 2013 coverage of the draft law (not opened, so not a source) describe a ceiling of TND 5,000, and the 1999 precedent (SRC-TG-927) also used a ceiling. A write-off of loans above a threshold would be unusual and may be a reporting error. The official text of Loi n° 2013-54 (Finance Law 2014) was not opened; the threshold is therefore unconfirmed.

resolvedSources.title: BNA : seulement 25 MDT des créances agricoles sont abandonnées
resolvedSources.extracts:
> n'ont pas dépassé les 25,5 millions de dinars (MDT)

English gloss: agricultural receivables written off by BNA on its own funds (first half 2023 accounts) did not exceed TND 25.5 million.

> Il s'agit de la loi n° 65-99 du 15 juillet 1999 et de la loi n° 2013-54, relative à la loi des finances de l'année 2014.

English gloss: the write-offs were made under Law 99-65 of 15 July 1999 and Law 2013-54 (Finance Law 2014).

resolvedSources.title: Dettes agricoles : voici ce que prévoit la nouvelle loi adoptée par le Parlement
resolvedSources.extracts:
Article of 11 March 2026 (author N.J.):

> environ 33.533 agriculteurs et entreprises agricoles sont concernés par ces situations d'endettement.

English gloss: about 33,533 farmers and agricultural enterprises are concerned by these debt situations.

> dont les créances sont classées en catégorie 4 auprès de la Banque centrale

English gloss: whose debts are classified in category 4 at the Central Bank.

> un rééchelonnement de la dette sur une durée maximale de sept ans, assorti d'une période de grâce d'une année

> la remise intégrale des pénalités et des intérêts de retard appliquées aux créances concernées

> versement préalable d'un montant équivalent à 5% du principal de la dette

> dans un délai compris entre un et six mois [...] les bénéficiaires pourront prétendre à une remise de 50% sur les montants dus [...] intérêts contractuels compris [...]

> Le texte a été adopté par 73 voix pour, deux abstentions et trois voix contre

English gloss: rescheduling over up to seven years with one grace year; full waiver of penalties and late interest; prior payment of 5% of principal; a 50% discount on amounts due for settlement within one to six months; adopted by 73 votes for, 2 abstentions, 3 against.

> par le passé, plusieurs mesures d'exonération ont été accordées aux entreprises agricoles

English gloss: in the past, several exemption measures were granted to agricultural enterprises.
resolvedSources.notes: Tier C press report on Law n° 2026-5 of 11 March 2026 (regularisation of unpaid agricultural debts). The official gazette text is recorded in SRC-TG-932. Other press (La Presse, 13 March 2026) gives the same rescheduling terms and adds a cut-off of debts unpaid before 30 September 2025 and an application deadline of 31 December 2026; that article was read but is not separately recorded.

resolvedSources.title: Tunisie: Crédits agricoles accrochés au-delà du rééchelonnement des dettes
resolvedSources.extracts:
Article of 16 March 2026 (author Lassâad Ben Ahmed):

> plus de 33.000 agriculteurs qui se sont vus exclure de tout financement bancaire

English gloss: more than 33,000 farmers excluded from any bank financing.

> estimées à 4,4 milliards de dinars, dont 21,5 % sont des créances classées

English gloss: farmers' debts estimated at TND 4.4 billion, of which 21.5% are classified (non-performing) claims.

> dont les crédits accordés à l'agriculture ne dépassent pas les 7% de son portefeuille

English gloss: (BNA) whose loans to agriculture do not exceed 7% of its portfolio.
resolvedSources.notes: Tier C. The article says the TND 4.4 billion / 21.5% figures were revealed at a parliamentary study day in January 2026. A separate Tunisie Numérique report on 12 January 2026 (SRC-TG-933) quotes BCT officials reporting agricultural credit outstanding of about TND 4,600 million at end-November 2025. The 4.4 billion figure is likely outstanding credit (including performing loans), not arrears; it should not be described as total farmer debt without that qualification.

resolvedSources.title: قانون عدد 5 لسنة 2026 مؤرخ في 11 مارس 2026 يتعلّق بتسوية الديون الفلاحية المتعثّرة (Loi n° 2026-5 du 11 mars 2026, JORT n° 28, p. 497)
resolvedSources.publisher: Journal Officiel de la République Tunisienne (copy hosted by the Assemblée des Représentants du Peuple)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Article 1 (الفصل الأول):

> تلتزم البنوك العمومية والخاصة بتسوية وضعية الديون البنكية للفلاحين والمؤسسات الناشطة في القطاع الفلاحي والمصنفة لدى البنك المركزي التونسي صنف 4 فما فوق، من خلال إعادة جدولة كامل أصل الدين وقيمة الفوائد التعاقدية الأصلية الموظفة، على مدة أقصاها 7 سنوات منها سنة إمهال وطرح خطايا التأخير شريطة دفع 5% من قيمة أصل الدين عند تقديم مطلب التسوية.
>
> وفي صورة خلاص كامل الدين دون جدولة، ينتفع المدين بطرح كلّ من خطايا التأخير و50% من قيمة الفوائد التعاقدية الأصلية الموظفة على أن يستوفي الخلاص في أجل أقصاه ستة أشهر من تقديم مطلب التسوية.

English gloss: public and private banks must settle the bank debts of farmers and agricultural enterprises classified by the Central Bank in category 4 or above, by rescheduling the full principal and the original contractual interest over at most 7 years including one grace year, and waiving late-payment penalties, on condition of paying 5% of the principal when applying. If the whole debt is paid without rescheduling within six months of the application, the debtor also gets a waiver of late penalties and of 50% of the original contractual interest.

Article 2 (الفصل 2):

> [...] يتولى البنك المركزي التونسي حذف كل التصنيفات البنكية السلبية [...]

> يتولى البنك المركزي التونسي حذف كل التصنيفات البنكية السلبية المتعلقة بالفلاحين والمؤسسات الفلاحية المنتفعة بهذا القانون بصفة آلية إثر المصادقة على اتفاقيات الجدولة أو الصلح مع البنوك.
>
> تستثنى من أحكام هذا القانون الديون محل تتبعات قضائية في جرائم فساد أو غسيل أموال إلا في صورة صدور حكم بات بالبراءة.

English gloss: the Central Bank automatically deletes all negative bank classifications of beneficiary farmers and agricultural enterprises once rescheduling or settlement agreements with banks are approved. Debts subject to prosecution for corruption or money laundering are excluded unless there is a final acquittal.

Article 3 (الفصل 3):

> يشمل هذا القانون الديون البنكية المتعّثرة المنصوص عليها بالفصل الأول من هذا القانون والمصنفة لدى البنك المركزي التونسي صنف 04 وما فوق قبل 30 سبتمبر 2025. ويجري العمل بأحكام هذا القانون إلى غاية 31 ديسمبر 2026.

English gloss: the law covers distressed bank debts classified in category 4 or above before 30 September 2025, and applies until 31 December 2026.

Footnote: adopted by the Assembly of the Representatives of the People on 10 March 2026.
resolvedSources.notes: Official gazette page (JORT n° 28 of 11 March 2026, p. 497), extracted from the PDF text layer; presentation-form Arabic letters normalised. Discrepancy with press: Business News (SRC-TG-930) reported a 50% discount "sur les montants dus" for early payment, whereas the law grants 50% of the original contractual interest only, plus late penalties. The law gives no count of beneficiaries and no amounts.

relatedItems.title: The 1986-1995 agricultural adjustment programme (PASA) removed most input subsidies but left administered wheat prices and the state offices' dual role in place
Price support and border protection favour cereals, milk and beef over Mediterranean crops and mostly benefit large farms; whether cereal growers are supported or taxed depends on the year
Rainfed cereal output swings with rainfall and collapsed in the 2023 drought, cutting the harvest by roughly two-thirds or more
The state cereal system (Office des Céréales monopoly, decreed prices, CGC subsidies) built in 1962-1971 now strains public finances and blunts market signals
Between 1961 and 2005 farms split into micro-holdings through inheritance while farm heads aged, and these small farms barely invest or borrow; no newer national data have been found
Collective land attribution and registration remain incomplete under the 2016 amendment, while evidence linking title gaps to small farmers’ bank-credit exclusion is thin and dated
Tunisia’s 2023 drought coincided with a 16.1% contraction in real agriculture, forestry and fishing value added in the revised INS accounts
